subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Assembly Line
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Assembly Line usable.

hook.text: Before Ford, building one car took over 12 hours. Each worker did almost everything.

buildup.text: Ford studied meatpacking plants where carcasses moved past workers on hooks—each person did one cut.

discovery.text: He reversed the idea: instead of moving workers, he moved the car past stationary workers.

twist.text: Build time dropped from 12 hours to 93 minutes. Costs plummeted and output exploded.

climax.text: Every manufacturer on earth eventually copied Ford's system. It reshaped all of modern industry.

punchline.text: Ford didn't invent the car. He invented how to build millions.

details.summary: Henry Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, reduced the time to build a Model T from 12 hours to 93 minutes, making mass production of affordable cars possible for the first time.
details.whyItMatters: The assembly line revolutionized not just automaking but all manufacturing. It enabled economies of scale that slashed prices and made consumer goods accessible to the working class.
takeaways: Production time dropped from 12 hours to 93 minutes per car
Workers performed one specialized task as cars moved past them
The Model T's price fell from $850 to under $300 over its run

faq.question: Did Ford invent the assembly line?
faq.answer: Ford adapted the concept from meatpacking plants and flour mills. His innovation was applying continuous flow production specifically to automobiles, perfecting the moving assembly line concept.

faq.question: Did workers enjoy assembly line work?
faq.answer: Many found the repetitive tasks monotonous and physically demanding. Ford's five-dollar day helped retain workers, but turnover remained high as laborers sought less grueling employment.
